The expected output requires the agent to (1) discover the customer's own kernel log group whose name does NOT begin with /aws/parallelcluster, (2) identify which stream carries kernel messages per node, (3) verify per-node whether that kernel log stream was actually live/arriving over the window, and (4) explicitly distinguish 'no Xid errors found in a proven-live log' from 'not observable because the stream was silent/missing' — critically, not reporting absence of Xids from a silent/missing stream as a healthy GPU signal.

The agent's response only scanned the ParallelCluster-prefixed log group (/aws/parallelcluster/distributed-training-triage-b200-...) and did not mention discovering or checking a separate customer kernel log group outside that prefix. It also did not verify whether the kernel-message stream itself was live (i.e., whether kernel lines were actually being emitted/ingested) versus just checking log groups exist. While the agent raised a good caveat about the health check possibly never calling nvidia-smi/DCGM (touching on the 'absence is only meaningful if something was watching' theme), this is a different and weaker check than confirming kernel-level log liveness per node across the window. The agent also flagged the SSM agent issue and the scale-to-zero timing gap, which are useful caveats, but these do not satisfy the specific requirement to verify kernel log stream liveness or to locate the separate customer kernel log group.

Overall, the agent gave a reasonable-sounding answer with some appropriate hedging, but it did not perform the specific diagnostic step described in the expected output — confirming kernel-level GPU logging was actually arriving from each node by locating and checking the correct kernel log stream (potentially in a differently-named log group). Thus it fails the core requirement of the expected output.
